Ashley: Quick q — trying to capture a short nsys trace to investigate weird kernel selection during KV cache warmup. I want minimal duration, trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt, but sampling seems to miss short kernels. Any practical flags or tricks?

Mike: Bracket with NVTX ranges around the warmup section and extend the sampling window. Sampling misses sub-ms kernels unless you either NVTX each call or increase the sample interval/duration.

Devon: Our go-to: drive a small warmup script that emits NVTX around each request, then run `nsys profile` with capture-range. Example pattern we use: run 8-12 warmup requests -> NVTX push for start/end -> `nsys profile -o warmup_trace --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx:warmup_start:warmup_end --stop-time=25s`

Sam: Quick note: `--sample=cpu` only captures CPU sampling. For correlating short CUDA kernels you want event tracing (cuda) + NVTX annotations. There's also `--sample-interval` in newer nsys to tweak sampling freq.

Jess: Concrete recipe that worked for our KV cache warmup perf regression triage:

1) Add NVTX around the per-batch warmup loop: `nvtxRangePushA("kv_warmup")` / `nvtxRangePop()`
2) Make the warmup perform a few slightly spaced calls (sleep 50-200ms) so kernels don't all coalesce
3) Run nsys like:

```
nsys profile -o traces/kv_warmup --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --capture-range=nvtx:kv_warmup:kv_warmup_end \
  --sample=cpu --stop-time=20s --force-overwrite
```
I often bump `--stop-time` to 30s for better sampling density.

Mike: Another trick — if kernels are extremely short, amplify them with a microbench that repeats the same code path repeatedly (so you get better statistical signal). Also try `--sample-interval=100us` if your nsys supports it.

Ashley: How do you keep trace size manageable? Our warmup traces hit 400-600MB quickly.

Devon: Capture only what you need: drop `osrt` if it's noisy, or avoid system call tracing. Use `--trace=cuda,nvtx` to cut noise. You can also post-process with `nsys export` and filter by NVTX ranges then discard raw .qdrep.

Sam: Correlate kernel names with sequence length / batch size via NVTX metadata. We push metadata like `nvtxPayload` with seq_len so the flame chart shows kernel vs seq_len clusters — super helpful for kernel selection bugs.

Jess: If you suspect sampling bias, run two captures: one with sampling (fast) and one full `--trace=cuda,nvtx` without CPU sampling to cross-check hotspots.

Ashley: Awesome, thanks everyone — I'll try the NVTX-bracketed capture + slightly longer stop-time and report back with the trace file.
